segments.voice: Yesterday, jnana met a person the size of a thumb and read it as Brahman, sought in the heart. Today, the last day in the sutras, and a lump of clay.
screen: `SPACE IN A REED IS STILL SPACE.`

segments.voice: Spring of senior year. Signatures fill the back of a yearbook, and every name is headed somewhere different: a college far away, a job, a gap year, the family business. Looking at a page like that, it's easy to see only the scattering. Ask where the world itself comes from, and a similar split seems natural: a maker over here, some stuff over there. A potter, and clay. Near the end of their first chapter, the Brahma Sutras take up exactly this. If Brahman is the source of everything, is Brahman the potter, or the clay?
screen: `EVERY NAME HEADED SOMEWHERE ELSE.` → `A MAKER, AND SOME STUFF?` → `THE POTTER, OR THE CLAY?`

segments.voice: The sutra's answer: both. Brahman is the material too, not only the maker. And it gives its reason from the Upanishads' own words. In the Chandogya, a father, Uddalaka, asks his son Shvetaketu whether he's learned the teaching by which the unheard becomes heard, the unknown known. Then the example. By one lump of clay, everything made of clay is known. The pot, the bowl, the lamp are names and shapes; the clay is what's real in them. Shankara presses the point. That promise, know one thing and know everything, only works if the one thing is what everything is made of. If Brahman were only the potter, knowing the potter wouldn't tell you the pots. The next sutra adds a clue. The texts say the source wished: may I be many. Nothing outside it is mentioned to become the many, so it becomes many from itself. That's where this run has been heading. Jnana, in Shankara's hands, isn't learning a long list of things. It's knowing the one clay, so the pots stop being strangers to each other. Ramanuja and Madhva read these same sutras differently, and their followers still do.
screen: `BOTH THE MAKER AND THE MATERIAL.` · `ONE LUMP OF CLAY, ALL CLAY KNOWN.` · `MAY I BE MANY.` · then, large: `THE POTS STOP BEING STRANGERS.`

segments.voice: Hold or look at one cup, bowl or mug near you. Take in its shape first, the rim, the handle, the chip if it has one. Then let the shape soften in your attention, and notice what it's made of, the same stuff as the other cups in the cupboard, wearing a different name.
Jnana: knowledge that frees. For Shankara, knowing the one clay, so the many are known.
For the road: jnana: the Brahma Sutras 1.1–1.4 with Shankara, where the pots stop being strangers. The sutras, complete.

howItsDone: In Advaita Vedanta, the clay example of the Chandogya Upanishad is often used to teach that Brahman is both the maker and the material of the world; Vishishtadvaita and Dvaita teachers read the same sutras in their own ways.

fork.setup: Uddalaka promises a teaching by which the unknown becomes known. you're Shankara. why does that promise need Brahman to be the clay, not only the potter?
options: knowing the potter wouldn't tell you the pots; knowing the clay does.
because potters are less important than the things they make.
it doesn't; the promise works either way.
fork.reveal: Know one thing and know everything only works if the one thing is what everything is made of. So the sutra says Brahman is the material too.

original.note: Sanskrit mrittika, clay or earth; the Chandogya's example of the one stuff in every pot.

what a scholar hears: Brahma Sutra 1.4.23–24: Brahman as material as well as efficient cause, so as not to break the Chandogya's promise and example (6.1.4), and from the wish 'may I be many'.

chat.meaning: The Chandogya's clay teaching: by one lump of clay all clay things are known; pots keep their names and shapes, and the clay is real in them.

Uddalaka.meaning: a father and teacher in the Chandogya Upanishad

Chandogya.meaning: an Upanishad with the teaching of the clay

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 6.1.1–6 (Uddalaka asks Shvetaketu about the teaching by which the unheard is heard; by one lump of clay all that is made of clay is known; the change is a name; the clay is real)
Chandogya Upanishad 6.2.3; Taittiriya Upanishad 2.6 (the source wished: may I be many)

Brahma Sutra 1.4.23–24 with Shankara's commentary (Brahman is the material cause as well as the efficient cause, so as not to contradict the promise and the example; and because of the teaching of reflection/wish)
